blocks.speaker: SPEAKER_19
blocks.text: Good evening, council members and city administration. My name is Brian Everett and I am here this evening to discuss about my least favorite topic, despite what you may think and how frequently I speak about it, which is road safety, street safety, pedestrian safety. In the time since last council meeting, there are two instances in the city that I'm aware of where vehicles have jumped the curb and hit things that are off of the street, one of them being Firehouse Park, where somebody jumped the curb, hit a telephone pole, an area where people play frequently, especially with the warmer weather, and St. Mary's from across the street has their recess. Additionally, in the last couple days, there was a car that hit and went into the salon across from Tiberio's. Apologize, I can't think of the name of it. I don't go to a lot of salons. But I think that this is indicative of issues with our street design. Irrespective of any traffic safety studies or understanding of traffic engineering or physics or anything like that, having two vehicles jump the curb and hit things that are off of the street should be enough to anecdotally realize that we have some problems with our street design. And I realize that nobody here on city council is at fault. Nobody here in the city administration or employee was here. This has been going on since the 1950s. And I would suggest that now is the time, if not well, past the time to begin the same incremental changes that made our streets more dangerous to make our streets more safe. We shouldn't have to rely on the perfect driver being out there. That person doesn't exist. There's 40,000 people a year in this country that are killed in traffic crashes. We shouldn't have to rely on extra safety forces being around to make somebody stop speeding or not speed. We should design streets that do not physically allow you to go fast enough to jump off of the street and hit a building. Thank you.
